prompt: What landform develops where two oceanic plates pull apart at a divergent boundary?

options.text: A mid-ocean ridge where rising magma builds new crust
A deep-sea trench where one plate sinks under another
A fold mountain belt formed by two colliding continents
A transform fault zone where plates slide horizontally

explanation: As oceanic plates pull apart, magma rises from the mantle, cools, and builds a mid-ocean ridge.

trap_notes.b: Deep-sea trenches form at convergent subduction zones, not divergent boundaries.
trap_notes.c: Fold mountains like the Himalayas form where two continental plates collide.
trap_notes.d: Transform boundaries slide sideways without creating new ocean ridges.
trap_notes.default: Divergent ocean plates pull apart, letting magma rise to form a mid-ocean ridge.

prompt: Why do volcanic mountain chains like the Andes form along ocean-continent edges?

options.text: Denser ocean crust subducts under land crust and triggers melting
Two continental plates pull apart and flood the gap with basalt
River sediments pile up at the coast and harden into granite peaks
Glaciers carve deep valleys and push rock upward into volcanoes

explanation: Dense oceanic crust sinks beneath lighter continental crust, releasing water that melts rock into magma.

trap_notes.b: Pulling apart creates rift valleys, not subduction-zone volcanic chains.
trap_notes.c: River sediments build deltas, not volcanic mountain ranges.
trap_notes.d: Glaciers erode mountains rather than generating volcanic magma.
trap_notes.default: Subduction of dense oceanic crust beneath continental crust fuels coastal volcanoes.

prompt: Which plate motion characterizes a transform boundary such as the San Andreas Fault?

options.text: Two plates grind sideways past each other along a fault
Two plates pull apart while magma erupts onto the seafloor
One oceanic plate plunges steeply beneath an island arc
Two continental plates crumple upward into a high plateau

explanation: At a transform boundary, plates slide horizontally past one another, storing stress that causes earthquakes.

trap_notes.b: Plates pulling apart with magma eruptions describe a divergent boundary.
trap_notes.c: An oceanic plate plunging beneath an island arc is a convergent boundary.
trap_notes.d: Continental collision crumpling upward is also a convergent boundary.
trap_notes.default: Transform boundaries involve horizontal sliding, as seen along the San Andreas Fault.

prompt: How does the Coriolis effect deflect moving winds and ocean currents in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.text: It curves them to the right of their path of motion
It curves them to the left of their path of motion
It pulls them straight toward the equator from both poles
It stops horizontal air flow at thirty degrees latitude

explanation: Earth's eastward rotation makes winds and currents curve right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern.

trap_notes.b: Deflection to the left occurs in the Southern Hemisphere, not the Northern.
trap_notes.c: Trade winds blow toward the equator, but Coriolis bends them sideways.
trap_notes.d: Sinking air at 30 degrees creates calm horse latitudes, not a Coriolis stop.
trap_notes.default: Coriolis deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

prompt: What drives the heavy summer monsoon rains across South Asia?

options.text: Moist ocean winds rush inward toward warm low-pressure land
Dry polar air sweeps south across the Himalayas to the sea
Cold ocean currents chill coastal air and block evaporation
High pressure over central India pushes dry air out to sea

explanation: In summer, South Asian land heats faster than the Indian Ocean, drawing humid sea air inland to drop heavy rain.

trap_notes.b: The Himalayas actually block cold polar air from entering India.
trap_notes.c: Cold currents cause coastal deserts, not heavy summer monsoon rains.
trap_notes.d: Winds blowing from land to sea describe the dry winter monsoon, not summer.
trap_notes.default: Summer heating creates low pressure over land, pulling wet Indian Ocean winds inland.

prompt: Why does a dry rain shadow form on the leeward side of a coastal mountain range?

options.text: Descending air warms up and holds moisture after losing rain upwind
Rising air cools down and condenses into heavy snow on the leeward side
Ocean currents reverse direction when they strike underwater ridges
Mountain glaciers absorb all water vapor from passing storm clouds

explanation: Moist air drops rain as it rises up the windward slope, then sinks, warms, and dries out on the leeward side.

trap_notes.b: Cooling and condensation happen on the windward side, creating wet slopes there.
trap_notes.c: Rain shadows are caused by air rising and sinking over mountains, not ocean currents.
trap_notes.d: Glaciers do not pull moisture out of storm clouds to create downwind deserts.
trap_notes.default: After air drops rain on the windward slope, it sinks and warms on the leeward side.

prompt: Which seasonal pattern defines a Mediterranean climate found in Greece and coastal California?

options.text: Warm, dry summers paired with mild, rainy winters
Hot, humid summers paired with freezing, snowy winters
Year-round heavy rainfall with no distinct dry season
Brief cool summers followed by eight months of permafrost

explanation: Mediterranean climates have dry, sunny summers and mild, wet winters that support olives, grapes, and scrub.

trap_notes.b: Hot humid summers and freezing winters describe humid continental climates.
trap_notes.c: Year-round heavy rain describes tropical rainforest or marine west coast climates.
trap_notes.d: Short cool summers and permafrost describe tundra climates.
trap_notes.default: Mediterranean climates are known for dry summers and mild, wet winters.

prompt: Why are tropical rainforest soils often poor for long-term row-crop farming after trees are cleared?

options.text: Heavy rain leaches minerals away and nutrients sit in living plants
Permafrost beneath the topsoil blocks roots from reaching water
Cold winter frosts kill soil microbes before organic matter decays
Salt crusts from dry winds coat the ground after every storm

explanation: Constant rain washes nutrients out of rainforest soil, while most nutrients are locked inside trees and plants.

trap_notes.b: Permafrost is found in polar tundra and taiga, not tropical rainforests.
trap_notes.c: Tropical rainforests stay warm year-round without freezing winter frosts.
trap_notes.d: Salt crusts form in arid deserts, not wet tropical basins.
trap_notes.default: Heavy rainfall leaches nutrients from rainforest soils once protective trees are cut.

prompt: Which biome forms a wide belt of needle-leaf conifers across Canada, Scandinavia, and Siberia?

options.text: The boreal forest, adapted to long cold winters
The tropical savanna, shaped by seasonal grass fires
The chaparral scrubland, shaped by dry summer heat
The temperate steppe, dominated by treeless prairies

explanation: The boreal forest, or taiga, stretches across high northern latitudes with spruce, pine, and fir trees.

trap_notes.b: Tropical savannas lie near the equator with scattered trees and tall grass.
trap_notes.c: Chaparral grows in warm Mediterranean regions, not subarctic belts.
trap_notes.d: Steppes are mid-latitude grasslands rather than subarctic conifer forests.
trap_notes.default: The boreal forest covers subarctic Canada, northern Europe, and Siberia.

prompt: What does a continental divide determine for precipitation falling on opposite mountain slopes?

options.text: Which ocean basin the runoff will eventually drain into
Whether the falling precipitation turns into rain or snow
Which hemisphere experiences summer during July
Where tectonic plates meet to trigger volcanic eruptions

explanation: A continental divide is a high ridge separating watersheds that flow toward different oceans or seas.

trap_notes.b: Temperature and elevation control rain versus snow, not a drainage divide.
trap_notes.c: Earth's axial tilt controls seasons, not mountain watershed boundaries.
trap_notes.d: Plate boundaries cause volcanoes, while divides govern river drainage.
trap_notes.default: A continental divide separates river systems flowing to different oceans.

prompt: How does an oxbow lake form along a mature river on a flat floodplain?

options.text: The river cuts off a tight meander loop and leaves it behind
A glacier carves a deep circular basin into solid granite
A volcanic crater fills slowly with rainwater over centuries
Ocean tides push sandbars across a rocky coastal fjord

explanation: As a river erodes the outside of a wide bend, it eventually slices straight through and isolates the old loop.

trap_notes.b: Glacier-carved basins form tarn or kettle lakes, not river oxbow lakes.
trap_notes.c: Water-filled volcanic craters are caldera lakes, such as Crater Lake.
trap_notes.d: Sandbars across coastal inlets form lagoons, not floodplain oxbow lakes.
trap_notes.default: Oxbow lakes are abandoned river meanders cut off from the main channel.

prompt: Which coastal feature is an estuary such as Chesapeake Bay?

options.text: A semi-enclosed bay where river freshwater mixes with ocean saltwater
A steep-walled canyon carved below sea level by melting glaciers
A ring-shaped coral reef enclosing a deep tropical lagoon
A high gravel ridge deposited along the edge of a melting ice sheet

explanation: An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal body where freshwater from rivers blends with salty ocean tides.

trap_notes.b: Steep glacier-carved coastal valleys flooded by the sea are fjords.
trap_notes.c: Ring-shaped coral reefs around tropical lagoons are atolls.
trap_notes.d: Gravel ridges left by melting ice sheets are moraines or eskers.
trap_notes.default: Estuaries are coastal transition zones where river freshwater meets ocean saltwater.

prompt: What geological process creates karst landscapes marked by sinkholes and underground caves?

options.text: Slightly acidic groundwater dissolves soluble limestone bedrock
Strong desert winds blast sand grains against basalt cliffs
Ocean waves pound granite headlands into tall sea stacks
Lava tubes cool quickly near the surface of shield volcanoes

explanation: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide to form weak carbonic acid, which slowly dissolves limestone into caves and sinkholes.

trap_notes.b: Wind-blown sand carves desert arches and yardangs, not karst caves.
trap_notes.c: Wave erosion on headlands creates sea stacks and cliffs, not inland sinkholes.
trap_notes.d: Lava tubes are volcanic features rather than dissolved limestone karst.
trap_notes.default: Karst topography forms when acidic groundwater dissolves limestone rock.

prompt: Why does Western Europe enjoy much milder winters than parts of Canada at the same latitude?

options.text: The warm Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift carry tropical heat northeast
The Alps block all cold Arctic winds from reaching the British Isles
Western Europe receives more direct sunlight hours in December
Dense European cities release enough waste heat to warm the Atlantic

explanation: Warm surface currents from the Gulf of Mexico flow northeast across the Atlantic, moderating Western Europe's winter air.

trap_notes.b: The Alps lie in southern Europe and cannot shield Britain from northern winds.
trap_notes.c: Places at the same latitude receive the same daylight hours in December.
trap_notes.d: Urban heat islands warm local cities, not an entire ocean basin or continent.
trap_notes.default: Warm Atlantic ocean currents keep Western Europe milder than Canada at equal latitudes.

prompt: What causes rapid population growth during Stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model?

options.text: Death rates fall sharply while birth rates remain high
Birth rates rise steeply while death rates climb even higher
Both birth rates and death rates stay low and nearly equal
Death rates exceed birth rates due to widespread aging

explanation: Cleaner water, sanitation, and vaccines cut death rates in Stage 2, while families still have many children.

trap_notes.b: If death rates climbed higher than birth rates, population would shrink, not boom.
trap_notes.c: Low, nearly equal birth and death rates describe Stage 4 stability.
trap_notes.d: Death rates exceeding birth rates due to aging describes Stage 5 decline.
trap_notes.default: Stage 2 booms because death rates drop before birth rates begin to fall.

prompt: Which demographic profile characterizes Stage 4 of the Demographic Transition Model?

options.text: Low birth rates and low death rates keep total growth near zero
High birth rates and high death rates keep total growth near zero
Falling death rates and high birth rates produce a sharp baby boom
High immigration and high infant mortality double the population

explanation: Stage 4 societies have low birth and death rates, high life expectancy, and slow or flat natural population growth.

trap_notes.b: High birth and high death rates characterize pre-industrial Stage 1.
trap_notes.c: Falling death rates with high birth rates characterize Stage 2.
trap_notes.d: Stage 4 countries have low infant mortality, not high infant mortality.
trap_notes.default: Stage 4 combines low birth rates with low death rates for slow population change.

prompt: What does a population pyramid with a very wide base and narrow top indicate about a country?

options.text: A high birth rate and a large share of young dependents
A shrinking workforce and a growing share of retirees
Zero natural population growth over the past fifty years
Heavy net out-migration of children under age five

explanation: A wide base shows many recent births, meaning a youthful population and rapid future growth.

trap_notes.b: A growing share of retirees creates a top-heavy or inverted pyramid.
trap_notes.c: Zero growth produces a column-like pyramid with straighter sides.
trap_notes.d: Out-migration of young children would narrow the base rather than widen it.
trap_notes.default: A wide pyramid base signals high birth rates and a young population.

prompt: Which example best illustrates a pull factor in human migration?

options.text: Abundant factory jobs and higher wages in a growing city
A multi-year drought destroying crops in a rural valley
Armed conflict forcing families to flee their home region
Rising sea levels flooding low-lying coastal farmland

explanation: Pull factors are attractive conditions in a destination, such as jobs, safety, or schools, that draw migrants in.

trap_notes.b: Crop-destroying drought is a push factor driving people away from home.
trap_notes.c: Armed conflict is a push factor forcing people to leave.
trap_notes.d: Coastal flooding is an environmental push factor, not a destination pull.
trap_notes.default: Pull factors attract migrants to a new place, while push factors drive them away.

prompt: What does the term brain drain describe in international migration?

options.text: Highly educated workers leaving their home country for better pay abroad
Retirees moving from cold northern cities to warm coastal resorts
Seasonal farmworkers crossing a border only during harvest months
Refugees returning home after a peace treaty ends a civil war

explanation: Brain drain happens when doctors, engineers, or scientists emigrate, reducing skilled talent in their home nation.

trap_notes.b: Retirees moving to warmer climates is amenity migration, not brain drain.
trap_notes.c: Temporary harvest workers are seasonal labor migrants.
trap_notes.d: Refugees going home after war is return migration or repatriation.
trap_notes.default: Brain drain is the loss of skilled, educated professionals to other countries.

prompt: What defines a primate city in urban geography?

options.text: A city more than twice as large as any other in its country
A planned capital built solely for government offices
A historic port abandoned after railroads replaced ships
A suburban ring of office parks along a highway beltway

explanation: A primate city dominates its nation's population, economy, and culture, outsizing the second city by over two to one.

trap_notes.b: Planned capitals like Brasilia or Canberra are forward capitals, not necessarily primate cities.
trap_notes.c: Abandoned ports are declining towns, not dominant national centers.
trap_notes.d: Suburban office rings along highways are edge cities, not primate cities.
trap_notes.default: A primate city is far larger and more dominant than every other city in its nation.

prompt: In Ernest Burgess's concentric zone model, which area sits at the very center of the city?

options.text: The central business district of offices and retail
The commuter zone of low-density suburban homes
The agricultural belt of dairy farms and orchards
The industrial corridor of heavy steel mills

explanation: Burgess placed the central business district at the core, surrounded by outward rings of factories and housing.

trap_notes.b: The commuter zone sits in the outermost ring of the Burgess model.
trap_notes.c: Farms belong to Von Thunen's agricultural model, not Burgess's city rings.
trap_notes.d: Factories sit in the zone just outside the central business district.
trap_notes.default: The central business district occupies Ring 1 at the core of the concentric zone model.

prompt: Which process is shown when immigrants bring a traditional cuisine to a new country?

options.text: Relocation diffusion, carried physically by moving people
Hierarchical diffusion, mandated first by national leaders
Stimulus diffusion, where only a logo is copied without the dish
Contagious diffusion, spreading online without anyone moving

explanation: Relocation diffusion occurs when people migrate and physically carry their language, food, or religion to a new place.

trap_notes.b: Hierarchical diffusion spreads from powerful hubs or leaders downward.
trap_notes.c: Stimulus diffusion adapts an underlying idea while changing its form.
trap_notes.d: Contagious diffusion spreads rapidly from person to person without migration.
trap_notes.default: Relocation diffusion happens when migrants carry cultural traits to new homes.

prompt: How does hierarchical diffusion differ from contagious diffusion?

options.text: It jumps from major hubs to smaller towns rather than neighbor to neighbor
It spreads only through rural villages while skipping major capitals
It requires entire populations to relocate across international borders
It blocks ideas from changing once they reach a new region

explanation: Hierarchical diffusion leaps between key cities or influential leaders before trickling down to smaller places.

trap_notes.b: Hierarchical diffusion starts in major hubs, not rural villages.
trap_notes.c: Mass migration across borders describes relocation diffusion.
trap_notes.d: Ideas often adapt as they spread; hierarchical describes the path, not rigidity.
trap_notes.default: Hierarchical diffusion moves from big hubs to smaller ones, unlike neighbor-to-neighbor spread.

prompt: In Von Thunen's agricultural model, why are dairy and fresh vegetables grown closest to the city?

options.text: They spoil quickly and cost more per mile to transport to market
They require huge open pastures that are cheapest near city centers
They grow poorly in rural soil and need urban factory pollution
They can be stored for years without refrigeration or spoilage

explanation: Before modern refrigeration, perishable milk and produce had to sit in Ring 1 to reach city buyers before spoiling.

trap_notes.b: Land near the city is expensive, not cheap; ranching sits in the outer ring.
trap_notes.c: Urban pollution harms crops rather than helping them grow.
trap_notes.d: Grain and livestock can travel farther because they do not spoil as fast.
trap_notes.default: Perishability and high transport cost keep dairy and produce in the innermost ring.

prompt: Why do farmers practicing shifting cultivation clear a new forest plot every few years?

options.text: Ash nutrients fade quickly, so farmers let old plots regrow
Heavy tractors compact the soil until no rain can enter
Winter blizzards bury tropical fields under deep snowdrifts
Commercial grain silos fill up and force crews to move north

explanation: After clearing and burning vegetation, crops thrive briefly on the ash, then farmers move on so the forest can recover.

trap_notes.b: Shifting cultivation uses hand tools rather than heavy commercial tractors.
trap_notes.c: Shifting cultivation occurs in warm tropical forests, not snowy regions.
trap_notes.d: Shifting cultivation is subsistence farming, not commercial silo-based grain farming.
trap_notes.default: Soil nutrients drop after a few harvests, so farmers rotate plots to let forest regrow.

prompt: What was a major result of the mid-twentieth-century Green Revolution in Asia and Latin America?

options.text: High-yield seeds and fertilizers sharply raised wheat and rice harvests
Farmers abandoned all irrigation canals in favor of dryland herding
Synthetic fertilizers were banned to restore medieval crop rotation
Urban factory workers returned to small hand-plowed subsistence plots

explanation: Dwarf high-yield wheat and rice varieties, paired with fertilizer and irrigation, boosted food output and averted famines.

trap_notes.b: The Green Revolution expanded irrigation rather than abandoning it.
trap_notes.c: Synthetic fertilizers were heavily used, not banned, during the Green Revolution.
trap_notes.d: The Green Revolution mechanized farming and freed labor for cities.
trap_notes.default: The Green Revolution paired high-yield seeds with fertilizer and irrigation to boost crops.

prompt: Why do similar tech or finance firms cluster in regions like Silicon Valley or Wall Street?

options.text: Agglomeration lets firms share skilled workers, suppliers, and ideas
Federal laws forbid software companies from opening outside California
Heavy raw ores like iron and coal are mined beneath downtown offices
Empty rural land in those districts costs less than farmland

explanation: Clustering creates agglomeration economies: firms benefit from nearby talent pools, specialized suppliers, and knowledge sharing.

trap_notes.b: No law restricts tech firms to one state; clustering is driven by cost and talent gains.
trap_notes.c: Software and finance rely on skilled labor and networks, not local iron mines.
trap_notes.d: Land in Silicon Valley and Manhattan is among the most expensive in the world.
trap_notes.default: Agglomeration saves costs by pooling specialized workers, suppliers, and ideas.

prompt: What role does a lingua franca such as Swahili in East Africa or English in aviation serve?

options.text: A common bridge language used for trade between different native groups
A secret dialect spoken only inside royal palace walls
A dead written script preserved solely on ancient stone monuments
A regional accent that prevents speakers from reading national laws

explanation: A lingua franca allows people with different mother tongues to communicate for commerce, travel, and diplomacy.

trap_notes.b: A lingua franca is widely used for public trade, not kept secret.
trap_notes.c: Living trade languages like Swahili and English are actively spoken daily.
trap_notes.d: A lingua franca enables broader communication rather than blocking it.
trap_notes.default: A lingua franca serves as a shared bridge language across different native speakers.

prompt: What is the main distortion on a Mercator world map projection?

options.text: Landmasses near the poles appear vastly larger than their true area
Countries along the equator appear stretched taller than continents
Compass directions bend into curved spirals across the oceans
The North and South Poles appear as tiny dots in the center

explanation: Mercator preserves compass angles for sea navigation, but stretches area near the poles, making Greenland look huge.

trap_notes.b: Mercator is most accurate in scale near the equator, not most distorted there.
trap_notes.c: Mercator was designed to keep compass bearings as straight lines.
trap_notes.d: The poles are stretched to infinity off the top and bottom of a Mercator map.
trap_notes.default: Mercator keeps true compass angles while exaggerating the size of polar landmasses.

prompt: Why do textbook publishers often choose the Robinson projection for world reference maps?

options.text: It balances size and shape distortions into a visually pleasing compromise
It keeps every continent free of shape or area distortion
It plots straight-line compass bearings for ocean ship captains
It enlarges Antarctica to twice the area of Eurasia for clarity

explanation: The Robinson projection is a compromise map that reduces extreme polar stretching while keeping continents recognizable.

trap_notes.b: No flat map of a round globe can eliminate all distortion at once.
trap_notes.c: Straight compass bearings are the strength of the Mercator projection.
trap_notes.d: Robinson shrinks polar exaggeration compared to Mercator rather than enlarging Antarctica.
trap_notes.default: Robinson is a compromise projection that balances area, shape, and distance errors.

prompt: What property does the Gall-Peters projection preserve accurately across the entire globe?

options.text: The true relative land area of continents and nations
The exact local shape of small islands near the equator
Straight-line compass angles for transatlantic airplanes
Equal walking distances between every pair of world capitals

explanation: Gall-Peters is an equal-area projection: it keeps landmass sizes proportional, though it stretches shapes vertically.

trap_notes.b: Gall-Peters stretches equatorial regions north-to-south, distorting their shape.
trap_notes.c: Mercator, not Gall-Peters, preserves compass angles.
trap_notes.d: No flat map preserves true distances between every pair of cities.
trap_notes.default: Gall-Peters is an equal-area projection that shows true relative continent sizes.

prompt: How does a Geographic Information System help city planners analyze flood risks?

options.text: By stacking elevation, river, and housing data in separate map layers
By launching weather balloons to steer hurricanes away from ports
By replacing all paper street signs with satellite radio beacons
By flattening Earth's curvature so every map is distortion-free

explanation: GIS stores, overlays, and analyzes multiple spatial data layers—like terrain, streets, and floodplains—to spot patterns.

trap_notes.b: GIS analyzes spatial data; it does not physically steer storms.
trap_notes.c: GPS provides navigation signals, whereas GIS maps and analyzes layered data.
trap_notes.d: GIS uses map projections, which still obey globe-to-flat geometry.
trap_notes.default: GIS overlays multiple spatial data layers to reveal geographic patterns and risks.

prompt: Which activity is an example of remote sensing in modern geography?

options.text: Using satellite sensors to track forest loss from orbit
Interviewing commuters at a downtown bus station
Digging soil pits with a shovel to measure clay depth
Reading nineteenth-century ship logs in a library archive

explanation: Remote sensing gathers information about Earth's surface from a distance using satellites, drones, or aircraft.

trap_notes.b: In-person interviews are field surveys, not remote sensing.
trap_notes.c: Digging soil pits is direct physical sampling on the ground.
trap_notes.d: Reading archives is historical research rather than sensor-based observation.
trap_notes.default: Remote sensing collects data from afar, typically via satellites or aircraft.

prompt: How does a large-scale map at 1:10,000 differ from a small-scale map at 1:10,000,000?

options.text: It covers a smaller area in much greater street-level detail
It covers an entire continent while hiding local roads
It omits all scale bars and compass roses for clarity
It shows higher mountain elevations in brighter red ink

explanation: 1/10,000 is a larger fraction than 1/10,000,000, so a large-scale map zooms in on a small area with rich detail.

trap_notes.b: Covering a continent with little local detail describes a small-scale map.
trap_notes.c: Large-scale maps include scale bars and legends just like small-scale maps.
trap_notes.d: Elevation coloring depends on map style, not on ratio scale.
trap_notes.default: A large-scale map zooms in closely on a small area to show fine detail.

prompt: Why is the Strait of Hormuz a critical global economic chokepoint?

options.text: Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil tankers pass through its narrow channel
It links the Mediterranean Sea directly to the North Atlantic Ocean
It carries most grain barges traveling down the Mississippi River
It provides the only ice-free rail tunnel under the Alps

explanation: Lying between Iran and Oman, the Strait of Hormuz connects Persian Gulf oil exporters to the open Indian Ocean.

trap_notes.b: The Strait of Gibraltar links the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean.
trap_notes.c: Mississippi grain barges exit through the Port of New Orleans, not Hormuz.
trap_notes.d: The Strait of Hormuz is a maritime waterway, not an Alpine rail tunnel.
trap_notes.default: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow sea exit for Persian Gulf oil shipments.

prompt: Which two major bodies of water does the Strait of Malacca connect for Asian shipping?

options.text: The Indian Ocean and the South China Sea
The Black Sea and the Aegean Sea
The Red Sea and the Mediterranean Sea
The Arctic Ocean and the Bering Sea

explanation: Running past Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore, the Strait of Malacca links the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.

trap_notes.b: The Bosporus and Dardanelles connect the Black Sea to the Aegean Sea.
trap_notes.c: The Suez Canal connects the Red Sea and the Mediterranean Sea.
trap_notes.d: The Bering Strait links the Arctic Ocean and the Bering Sea.
trap_notes.default: The Strait of Malacca is the key sea lane between the Indian Ocean and South China Sea.

prompt: How did opening the Suez Canal in 1869 reshape maritime trade between Europe and Asia?

options.text: Ships bypassed southern Africa by sailing between the Mediterranean and Red Seas
Ships crossed Central America instead of rounding Cape Horn
Icebreakers cleared a winter route across northern Siberia
River locks lifted ocean freighters over the Rocky Mountains

explanation: Egypt's Suez Canal linked the Mediterranean and Red Seas, cutting thousands of miles off voyages around Africa.

trap_notes.b: Crossing Central America describes the Panama Canal, opened in 1914.
trap_notes.c: Siberian sea lanes lie in the Arctic, far from the Suez Canal.
trap_notes.d: No canal crosses the Rocky Mountains.
trap_notes.default: The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean and Red Seas, avoiding the Cape of Good Hope.

prompt: Why does the Panama Canal rely on a system of freshwater locks?

options.text: To raise and lower ships over Gatun Lake above sea level
To flush icebergs out of the Caribbean Sea each spring
To block Pacific saltwater from reaching the Mediterranean
To generate enough tidal power to light all of South America

explanation: Panama's interior sits well above sea level, so locks lift ships up to Gatun Lake and lower them back down.

trap_notes.b: The tropical Caribbean Sea has no icebergs.
trap_notes.c: The Panama Canal links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, not the Mediterranean.
trap_notes.d: The locks are built for ship elevation, not continental power generation.
trap_notes.default: Locks lift ships up to Gatun Lake and lower them back to sea level across Panama.

geo.label: United Nations Law of the Sea

prompt: Under the UN Law of the Sea, what rights does a coastal nation hold in its Exclusive Economic Zone?

options.text: Sole rights to fish, drill, and mine within 200 nautical miles
Power to ban foreign cargo ships from passing 500 miles offshore
Ownership of all international airspace above the mid-ocean
Authority to tax inland rivers inside neighboring countries

explanation: An Exclusive Economic Zone extends up to 200 nautical miles offshore, giving coastal states control of marine resources.

trap_notes.b: Foreign ships retain freedom of navigation through another nation's EEZ.
trap_notes.c: EEZs cover marine resources up to 200 nautical miles, not mid-ocean airspace.
trap_notes.d: EEZs apply to coastal ocean waters, not neighboring inland rivers.
trap_notes.default: An EEZ gives a coastal state resource rights out to 200 nautical miles.

prompt: What major economic challenge do landlocked countries such as Bolivia and Chad face?

options.text: Higher shipping costs from relying on neighbors' ports and transit roads
Frequent tsunami damage to their deep-water container terminals
Inability to grow any grain crops without direct ocean frontage
Mandatory bans on joining regional trade agreements or air routes

explanation: Without a seacoast, landlocked states depend on neighbors' railways, highways, and ports, raising trade costs.

trap_notes.b: Landlocked countries have no ocean coastline or deep-water seaports.
trap_notes.c: Agriculture depends on soil and climate, not on having a seacoast.
trap_notes.d: Landlocked states actively join trade pacts and operate international airports.
trap_notes.default: Lacking a coastline forces landlocked countries to pay transit costs through neighbors.

prompt: Identify this major arid region from the three clues.
clues: I am a vast subtropical desert shaped by sinking dry air near 25 degrees north latitude.
I stretch across eleven countries from the Atlantic coast to the Red Sea.
I border the Mediterranean Sea to the north and the semi-arid Sahel to the south.

options.text: The Sahara Desert
The Gobi Desert
The Atacama Desert
The Kalahari Desert

explanation: The Sahara spans North Africa from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, bordering the Sahel on the south.

trap_notes.b: The Gobi is a cold mid-latitude desert in Mongolia and northern China.
trap_notes.c: The Atacama lies along the Pacific coast of northern Chile.
trap_notes.d: The Kalahari sits in southern Africa, not north of the Sahel.
trap_notes.default: The Sahara is Earth's largest hot desert, spanning North Africa.

prompt: Identify this river system from the three clues.
clues: I am one of the longest rivers on Earth, flowing generally from south to north.
My two main tributaries, the White and Blue branches, meet at Khartoum.
I empty through a fertile fan-shaped delta into the eastern Mediterranean Sea.

options.text: The Nile River
The Congo River
The Tigris River
The Niger River

explanation: The White and Blue Nile join at Khartoum in Sudan and flow north through Egypt to the Mediterranean.

trap_notes.b: The Congo River flows west into the Atlantic Ocean.
trap_notes.c: The Tigris flows southeast through Iraq into the Persian Gulf.
trap_notes.d: The Niger flows in a great arc through West Africa to the Gulf of Guinea.
trap_notes.default: The Nile flows north from East Africa to its Mediterranean delta.

prompt: Identify this mountain system from the three clues.
clues: I rose when two continental tectonic plates collided without subducting.
I form a natural wall blocking icy winter air from sweeping into South Asia.
I stretch across Nepal and Bhutan and contain Mount Everest.

The Andes Mountains
The Ural Mountains
The Atlas Mountains

explanation: The Indian and Eurasian collision pushed up the Himalayas, home to Mount Everest.

trap_notes.b: The Andes run along western South America above a subduction zone.
trap_notes.c: The Urals are an ancient range dividing Europe from Asia in Russia.
trap_notes.d: The Atlas Mountains lie across northwestern Africa.
trap_notes.default: The Himalayas formed from India colliding with Eurasia and hold Mount Everest.

prompt: Identify this biome from the three clues.
clues: I am a tropical broadleaf forest receiving heavy rainfall every month of the year.

The Congo Rainforest
The Boreal Taiga
The Pantanal Wetland

trap_notes.c: The Boreal Taiga is a cold northern conifer forest.
trap_notes.d: The Pantanal is a tropical wetland south of the Amazon forest.
trap_notes.default: The Amazon Rainforest is Earth's largest tropical rainforest, centered in Brazil.

prompt: Identify this marine feature from the three clues.
clues: I am a massive underwater ecosystem built by tiny calcium-secreting coral polyps.

I stretch over two thousand kilometers off the northeast coast of Queensland, Australia.

The Mariana Trench
The Sargasso Sea
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge

trap_notes.c: The Sargasso Sea is an open-ocean gyre in the North Atlantic.
trap_notes.d: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a divergent plate boundary down the Atlantic.
trap_notes.default: The Great Barrier Reef lies off northeastern Australia.

prompt: Identify this tectonic zone from the three clues.
clues: I form a horseshoe-shaped belt containing roughly three-quarters of Earth's volcanoes.

I rim the Pacific Ocean from New Zealand through Japan and Alaska to Chile.

The East African Rift
The Alpine-Himalayan Belt

trap_notes.d: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs down the center of the Atlantic Ocean.

prompt: Identify this maritime chokepoint from the three clues.
clues: I am a narrow sea passage less than fifteen kilometers wide at my tightest point.

I serve as the only natural water link between the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea.

The Strait of Hormuz
The English Channel
The Strait of Magellan

The Bab el-Mandeb

The Great Salt Lake

The Edwards Plateau

The Mojave Desert
The Namib Desert
The Patagonian Steppe
